land.text: the Black Sea coast from the Bzyb to the Ingur, the Sharvashidzes' principality after the 1463 defeat of George VIII at Chikhori

predecessors.note: The infobox lists the Kingdom of Georgia and the Kingdom of Imereti as predecessors; the page says that in 1490 'Abkhazia became part of Imereti'.

land.text: the principality, absorbed into the Russian Empire in 1864 after the Caucasian War; Prince Michael renounced his rights in November 1864

successors.note: The infobox lists the Ottoman Empire as a second successor without saying what it took. Cliopatria's row ends in 1829, 35 years before the page's end.

capitals.name: Zupu (Lykhny)
capitals.note: Infobox: capital Zupu (Lykhny), no years given. The Lykhny page says only that the palace ruins were 'used as a residence by the princes of Abkhazia'; the Sukhumi page does not call Sukhumi a capital of the Abkhazian princes.

rulers.name: Putu Sharvashidze
rulers.note: All reigns are 'c.' dates from the page's list; the list begins c. 1580 (Putu) although the infobox gives Rabia Sharvashidze, c. 1451-1465, as the first prince; 1465-1580 is not listed.

rulers.name: Kelesh Ahmed-Bey Sharvashidze
rulers.note: The page gives Sunni Islam dynastic rule 1780-1810.

rulers.name: Aslan-Bey Sharvashidze
rulers.note: Assassinated his father on 2 May 1808; replaced by the Russians on 2 July 1810.

rulers.name: Mikhail Sharvashidze
rulers.note: Forced to renounce his rights in November 1864 and move to Voronezh.

correction.text: Abkhazia as Cliopatria's first shape, carried back to 1463

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria starts Abkhazia in 1468; the infobox says 'Established: 1463' and the text that the Sharvashidzes 'joined a rebellion against King George VIII, who was defeated at Chikhori in 1463, which led to the principality's founding'. The 1468 shape is carried back unchanged.

6,066 km2, a coastal strip from the Bzyb to the Ingur. The page gives no area to compare. 'In 1490, Georgia was split by treaty, and Abkhazia became part of Imereti' (an overlordship, recorded in the Imereti dossier); the shape is not changed by it.

5,829 km2 (-4%): a small southern strip goes. 'In the 1570s, the Ottoman navy seized the fort of Tskhumi and turned it into Suhum-Kale' (Abkhazia page); the Sukhumi page says Tskhumi, 'contested between the princes of Abkhazia and Mingrelia, ... finally fell to the Turks in the 1570s'. Neither page gives the year; 1572 is Cliopatria's.

correction.text: Abkhazia without Tskhumi (Suhum-Kale, Ottoman since the 1570s), kept through 1579-1611

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1579-1611, which Cliopatria leaves empty (its Ottoman row probably covers it). Nothing on the page ends the principality: the ruler list runs unbroken from Putu Sharvashidze, c. 1580-1620. The 1572 shape is kept, with the Ottomans holding Suhum-Kale.
5,829 km2, the 1572 shape again. The page is silent on 1612-1699; the border conflicts with Mingrelia are only given as 'throughout the 16th-18th centuries'. Unverified: page silent.

10,255 km2 (+76%): the Ghalidzga-Enguri strip is added. 'After Zegnak's death around 1700, his principality was divided among his sons' (Abkhazia page); Samurzakano page: 'in 1705 three brothers of the Abkhazian ruling family, surnamed Chachba' divided it, the third taking 'the southern part (from the Ghalidzga to the R. Enguri)', 'roughly equivalent to the modern Gali District'. So the strip is Abkhazian by 1705; the pages do not say it was taken from Mingrelia, and Cliopatria's Mingrelia loses 4,900 km2 in the same year.

8,714 km2 (-15%): the southernmost strip (south of 42.50N) is cut. The pages are silent; the same year Cliopatria's Mingrelia and Guria lose their western coast and an Ottoman row appears beside Mingrelia, so an Ottoman gain is the likeliest cause. Unverified: page silent.
8,667 km2, a 0.5% change that the pages do not explain. The Solomon I page has him 'crushed the Ottoman-sponsored insurrection in Abkhazia in 1779', with no territorial result.

10,232 km2 (+18%): the southern strip is back. No page dates it. The Abkhazia page has Sunni Islam dynastic rule from 1780 under Kelesh Ahmed-Bey; whether this bears on the strip is not said. Unverified: page silent.

9,852 km2 (-4%). 'On July 2, 1810, Russian Marines stormed Suhum-Kale and installed Sefer-Bey (1810-1821) in place of Aslan-Bey' (Abkhazia page); the Treaty of Bucharest left Russia holding 'Sukhum-Kale on the Abkhazian coast' (Russo-Turkish War page). The small loss in 1811 is read as that enclave.
9,758 km2 for 1812-1827; the 1812 Treaty of Bucharest 'Russia retained Sukhum-Kale on the Abkhazian coast'. No change on the Abkhazia page between 1812 and 1827.

9,758 km2 for 1828-1829. Cliopatria ends the row in 1829, but the principality lived to 1864; see the new keyframe below. 'The next Russo-Turkish war (1828-1829) strengthened Russia's position and split the Abkhaz elite along religious lines.'

correction.text: the principality as it stood in 1828, carried on to 1863

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1830-1863: the page has Prince Michael (1822-1864) ruling to November 1864, 'absorbed into the Russian Empire in 1864 after the Caucasian War'. The 1828 shape is carried forward unchanged; the land is a Russian vassal (the suzerain's dossier records the tint), and the 1853-1856 Russian evacuation is listed under wars.

region.text: the Sharvashidzes' coast between the Bzyb and the Ingur, seat at Zupu (Lykhny)

ledger.note: 1463: the Sharvashidzes found the Principality of Abkhazia. 'During the civil war of the 1450s, the Sharvashidzes joined a rebellion against King George VIII, who was defeated at Chikhori in 1463, which led to the principality's founding.' Infobox: 'Established: 1463'.

region.text: the fort of Tskhumi, renamed Suhum-Kale

ledger.note: 1570s: the Ottomans seize Tskhumi. 'In the 1570s, the Ottoman navy seized the fort of Tskhumi and turned it into Suhum-Kale.' The page names only the decade; 1572 is Cliopatria's shape change, and the Sukhumi page adds that Tskhumi had been 'contested between the princes of Abkhazia and Mingrelia'.

region.text: the southern part of Abkhazia 'from the Ghalidzga to the R. Enguri', roughly the modern Gali District

ledger.note: c. 1700-1705: the Ghalidzga-Enguri strip passes to the Abkhazian house. 'in 1705 three brothers of the Abkhazian ruling family, surnamed Chachba' divided their land, 'the third, Murzaqan, the southern part (from the Ghalidzga to the R. Enguri)'; the page says Samurzakano 'was established as a fief ... in the early 18th century'. The pages do not say the strip was taken from Mingrelia: that is read from Cliopatria, where Mingrelia loses 4,900 km2 in 1700 as Abkhazia gains 4,400. Year 1700 is Cliopatria's.

region.text: the strip of coast between 42.37N and 42.50N lost from the 1700 shape, near the Ingur mouth

ledger.note: 1727: a southern coastal strip leaves the Abkhazian shape (-1,540 km2). Page silent. Read as an Ottoman gain because Cliopatria's Mingrelia and Guria lose their western coast in the same year and an Ottoman row appears beside Mingrelia from 1727.

region.text: the strip of coast between 42.37N and 42.50N lost in 1727, near the Ingur mouth

ledger.note: 1788: the strip lost in 1727 returns (+1,570 km2). Page silent. Context from the page: Kelesh Ahmed-Bey (c. 1780-1808) was Muslim, and the Solomon I page has an 'Ottoman-sponsored insurrection in Abkhazia' crushed in 1779; the Ottoman counterpart is a reading.

region.text: Suhum-Kale, stormed by Russian Marines and kept by Russia

ledger.note: 2 July 1810: Russian Marines storm Suhum-Kale and install Sefer-Bey. 'On July 2, 1810, Russian Marines stormed Suhum-Kale and installed Sefer-Bey (1810-1821) in place of Aslan-Bey.' Russia kept the town (Treaty of Bucharest, 1812, 'Russia retained Sukhum-Kale on the Abkhazian coast'); Cliopatria's shape loses 380 km2 in 1811 and 95 more in 1812. That the town left the princes' domain is a reading from the shape; the page is silent on its status after the storming.

region.text: the whole principality, annexed after Prince Michael's renunciation in November 1864

ledger.note: 1864: Russia ends the Principality of Abkhazia. 'Russia subjugated the western Caucasus highlanders in 1864'; 'In November 1864, Prince Michael was forced to renounce his rights and move to Voronezh.' The page's infobox: disestablished 1864; succeeded by the Russian Empire.

wars.name: Russo-Turkish War (1806-1812)
wars.outcome: Russia stormed Suhum-Kale in 1810 and, at Bucharest (28 May 1812), 'retained Sukhum-Kale on the Abkhazian coast' while Turkey regained Poti, Anapa and Akhalkalaki.
wars.note: The war page does not date the storming; the Abkhazia page gives 2 July 1810. Abkhazian princes were split: Aslan-Bey pro-Ottoman until the Russians replaced him. No contest events: the fort changed hands once.

wars.name: Russo-Turkish War (1828-1829)
wars.outcome: 'Strengthened Russia's position and split the Abkhaz elite along religious lines'; the Treaty of Adrianople is not mentioned on the Abkhazia page.

wars.name: Crimean War
wars.outcome: 'During the Crimean War (1853-1856), Russian forces evacuated Abkhazia, and Prince Michael (1822-1864) reportedly switched to the Ottomans.'
wars.note: The page gives no dates for the evacuation or its end; no occupation events are recorded.

wars.name: Caucasian War
wars.outcome: 'Russia subjugated the western Caucasus highlanders in 1864' and Prince Michael was forced to renounce his rights in November 1864, ending the principality.
wars.note: Infobox: 'Caucasian War: 1817-64'. The principality itself was Russia's vassal for most of the war; the page records no front on its land.

certainty.note: A coastal principality whose inland limit lies in the Caucasus foothills and whose southern limit moved with the Mingrelian and Ottoman frontiers; no treaty or survey lines on the pages. The fort of Sukhumi (Tskhumi / Suhum-Kale) is the one fixed point.

notes: Page budget: up to 5, six opened (Lykhny only for the capital's coordinates). Infobox area absent, so no area comparison. Cliopatria: the row ends in 1829 though the principality ends in 1864 (infobox: disestablished 1864; Prince Michael renounced in November 1864); a new keyframe covers 1830-1863. No shape for 1579-1611 (new keyframe). The 1727 loss, the 1788 gain and the 1811 loss are Cliopatria shape changes that no page explains: they are recorded at confidence 1 with Ottoman and Russian counterparts as readings. Vassalage for the suzerain dossiers: Imereti (1490, 'Abkhazia became part of Imereti'; Imereti dossier records it); Ottoman Empire (Suhum-Kale from the 1570s; 'a pro-Ottoman orientation briefly prevailed' in 1808; the page gives no tribute dates); Russian Empire from 2 July 1810 (Sefer-Bey installed) to 1864. Cliopatria's Russian Empire row neighbours Abkhazia 1775-1829 and its Ottoman row 1612-1811. The infobox lists the Ottoman Empire as a successor beside Russia, unexplained. The page's ruler list is 'c.' throughout. Region names the gazetteer may lack: Samurzakano (region, the Gali District). The Abkhaz-Mingrelian 'border conflicts' of 'the 16th-18th centuries' are undated on the page and not ledgered.
